Shock redefinition: the market-flow trigger and the MM population

One catalogue of 915 market events, defined on extreme 30-minute net taker flow. The HYPE MM population against matched non-event controls, who absorbs the flow and who the shock rule flags, and what an alternative one-sided taker rule selects instead.

WindowHYPE perpetual, 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30 UTC
Price gatePrimary: overall-p95 absolute (168 bps). Sensitivity: weekly-relative class

Summary

Symbols used on this page (main)

Symbols used on this page (main)

  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • HYPE MM: a wallet the project's daily label model (v5d) classes as a HYPE market maker on that date.
  • Active MM: a labelled HYPE MM with at least one post-only (ALO) fill in the 2 hours before the event and at least one fill inside it.
  • sig24: the MM's own position scale over the 24 hours before t0, in HYPE, never below $12,500 of HYPE.
  • Shocked: the MM's position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 of its own sig24.
  • Absorption side, exit side: the maker side the event's takers trade against; the exit side is the other one.
  • Control window: the same clock time and length on the nearest date with no event nearby.
  • PRE2H, PRE30, POST: PRE2H is the 2 hours ending at t0; PRE30 the last 30 minutes before t0; POST the 2 hours after t1.
  • Markout M30, M60, M120: a fill's value against the mid 30, 60 or 120 minutes later, in bps; positive is favorable.
  • Roster: the ten named HYPE MMs, MM01 to MM10, of the earlier per-wallet shock study.
  • Forced, voluntary flow: forced flow is taker USD from liquidations and auto-deleveraging (ADL); voluntary flow is all other taker USD. A victim is the wallet that was force-closed.
  • Quantile cells: a cell with five numbers is p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95; with three, p25 / p50 / p75.
Flow is absorbed broadly; a few already-large MMs end the event shocked.The median event has 115 MMs with absorption-side maker fills and 5 shocked MMs. The five already held larger positions before the event: median |position| 1,752 HYPE against 254 for the rest. Inside one wallet their resting size was close to even across the two sides (§4.3). (§4)
A big price move is a fixed cutoff, not one relative to the week.An event is a big price move when the mid moves at least 168 bps from event start to event end, the p95 of all half-hour moves in the sample. A cutoff relative to each week would reclassify 163 events and change no event time. (§3)
A price trigger (extreme return) and the flow trigger (extreme net taker flow) flag different half hours.With both flagging the same number of half hours, about a third of the flow trigger's half hours are also price-trigger half hours. The price trigger's events overlap 31% of the 181 roster inventory shocks (recall), against 58% for the flow trigger. (§3.4)
Matched controls turn several apparent responses into ordinary market making.915 control windows at the same clock times carry the same measurements. They show no quoting lean to one side, no inventory move of shock size and no quoting shift after the window. (§4)
Across all active MMs, position scale predicts inventory shocks; trading activity does not.A wallet’s shock rate (how often it is shocked across events) has Spearman correlation +0.65 with its median |position| before events and +0.08 with its lifetime trades per bin, every date included. Much of the +0.65 is mechanical: the position scale in the shock rule has a fixed dollar floor. The +0.08 has no such issue. (§5.4)
A large sweep and the lasting price change are a second apart.A sweep is one taker order that fills through several price levels. The second that holds a $1m sweep ends near where it began. The price moves in the next second, once the best bid and ask have been refilled with small size. (§6.6)
Equity is flat at the median and wide in the tails.Equity is the whole account value. The median change for shocked MMs is +0.13% at event end and +0.15% at +6 h. 10.2% of shocked MMs, counted once per event, are below −5% at +6 h, every date included. Snapshots are 2 to 5.5 hours apart. (§4.7)
The wallets that absorb the most flow are usually not the wallets the shock rule flags.In 38.4% of events none of the five biggest absorbers (the MMs with the most absorption-side maker USD) is shocked. Their position change is a median 48.9 times that of the event’s median other MM, in HYPE. Their own position scale is also the event’s largest, so the change is only 2.2 times that scale. For 73.9% of them the position never reaches 3 times the scale at any minute. (§8)
A side-surge rule adds half hours that rarely hold a roster shock.The side-surge rule flags a half hour when taker buys alone or taker sells alone are extreme; the net-flow rule flags it when buys minus sells are extreme. Matched on event count, 595 side-surge events overlap a net-flow event and 327 overlap none: half hours in which both sides traded heavily and the net stayed small. Those 327 contain 8 of the 181 roster shocks, against 87 in the 595 overlapping events. (§9)

This page reads the taker-imbalance events, |zNET| ≥ 3.70 (set 1). The other definition, the 922 one-sided taker surges (set 3, section 9), is on its own page. Event studies holds sections 6, 7, 13 and 14, and Unwinders holds sections 4.4 and 10 to 12. Section, table and figure numbers are unchanged, so a reference reads the same on every page.

Each finding shows its headline. Click one to read the explanation.

Notation and shared definitions

Symbols and shared terms

Shared terms are defined here, and each section repeats in a few words the terms it uses. Terms specific to one section stay with it: the market trigger in §3.1, the population and event-time measures in §4.1, the early/late split in §4.4, the lifetime MM profile variables in §5.1.

Wallets, labels and codes

  • HYPE MM (v5d). A wallet that v5d, the project's daily wallet label model, calls a HYPE market maker on a given date. The label is per date, so a wallet can be an MM on some dates and not on others, and every count of "labelled MMs" is a count on that event's date. §4 uses the actively market-making MMs defined in §4.1 and §5 the labelled MMs that pass its activity screen, with no roster restriction.
  • The roster ten. The ten HYPE market makers of the earlier roster study (Exp7), written MM01 to MM10 throughout. The earlier per-wallet shock study (Exp8) detected the 181 roster shocks on these ten wallets. §3 scores each market rule by how many of the 181 it finds (recall and lift). In this report the roster is a comparison reference and a source of worked examples. §4 and §5 measure the whole labelled population. §6 and §7 name roster wallets because they are the shocked MMs in those two events.
  • Wallet codes. MM01–MM10 are the roster ten. T01–T10 are the largest taker wallets of a tick replay. X01–X06 are the largest non-roster makers in the liquidation tick replay. V01 is the largest liquidation victim. A code is fixed within a section. The same code can name a different wallet in another section; the note at the end of §7.5 explains the two code sets of event B. Roster MM, other MM and non-MM are wallet classes, not codes: other MM means labelled by v5d but not on the roster, non-MM means not labelled a HYPE MM on that date.

Fills and orders

  • Grouped fill, grouped trade. One row per taker order's execution against the book, with its level-by-level fills aggregated, from the grouped_trade_oid fill table. "Trades" counts these rows and "volume" is their USD notional, so one order that swept 200 levels is one trade.
  • Maker and taker. A fill is a taker (crossed) fill when the wallet's own order crossed the spread to take liquidity, and a maker fill otherwise. Taker share is crossed fill USD divided by all fill USD over whatever group is named.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC. Time-in-force. ALO is add-liquidity-only, a post-only order the venue rejects if it would cross; IOC is immediate-or-cancel; GTC is good-till-cancelled. "No market orders" means no unpriced immediate order was used.
  • What the order-state measures can see. Non-trigger limit orders only (ALO and GTC), from placement to their last status record; orders still open when the data end are dropped. The venue records a modify-in-place as a cancel plus a new order, so one modification counts as one cancel and one submit. This is why cancels per submit is near 1 for most MMs.
  • Liquidation, ADL, forced and voluntary. A liquidation is the venue force-closing a position; ADL (auto-deleveraging) is the venue closing a position against other accounts when a liquidation cannot fill. Forced flow is liquidation plus ADL taker USD; voluntary flow is all other taker USD. A victim is the wallet whose position was force-closed, and a victim's leg is a taker leg.

Prices, clocks and windows

  • bps. One basis point is 0.01%, so 100 bps is 1%. Every bps figure is measured against the reference price named beside it; where a level matters the report gives dollars as well.
  • Strict-pre. ts_bookdiff_lt is the book state strictly before the events carried at a timestamp; ts_bookdiff_le is the state after them. Every price in §6 and §7 is strict-pre unless it is named as an after-event price. A mid quoted at a trade's millisecond is therefore the book the trade hit, not the book it left behind.
  • The 5-minute bin-label offset. Exp8 catalogue timestamps are 5-minute bin labels and the corresponding clock window is the label plus five minutes, because the 5-minute position is an end-of-bin level. §15 states the consequences; every window in §6 and §7 already carries the offset.
  • Episode. Exp8's grouping of roster shocks that overlap in time into one market episode; one episode can contain several roster shocks. Event A is episode 89 (the tick replay in §6) and event B is episode 100 (the tick replay in §7).

Markouts

  • Markout Mk. For a fill at price p and size v, with d=+1 for a buy and d=−1 for a sell, Mk=d (midt+k−p) v in dollars: what the fill is worth marked to the mid k minutes later. A group of fills is quoted in bps of the fills' own notional as 104∑jMk,j/∑jpjvj, signed so that positive is favorable to the wallet. k is 30, 60 or 120 minutes, written M30, M60, M120. A negative maker markout means the mid kept moving against the side the wallet was filled on.

Replay conventions (§6 and §7)

  • W_focus. The shortest interval inside the replay's full analysis window that contains 80% of the trough-to-peak tick mid move. The rule gives 212 s in event A and 1,547 s, the whole move, in event B.
  • The surge-onset rule. The first second at which the 30-second rolling sum of hit-side taker USD reaches three times the trailing 6-hour p95 of that same statistic. §6.2 records why a per-second-median version cannot be used: 70% of baseline seconds carry no hit-side trade, so the median is $0 and the first ordinary trade reaches the threshold.
  • Baseline hour. The hour of the analysis window before the main price move starts. "Baseline-hour p95" and "baseline-hour low" are that hour's statistics, and a coin trading below its baseline-hour low is the new-low marker used in §7.3.
  • Levels swept and deepest walk. Levels swept is the number of distinct book price levels a taker order consumed. Deepest walk is the distance in bps from the strict-pre mid to the furthest level a single order reached.
  • Resting age. Time from an order's placement to the moment it was hit or cancelled. It separates a quote that was just re-posted from a stale order the price ran through.
  • Reaction latency (the §10 rule). Time from the taker-surge onset minute until the wallet's hit-side quoting first does either of two things: drops its resting hit-side size to 50% or less of its value at onset, or widens its best hit-side quote distance by 10 bps or more from its value at onset. Whichever fires first sets the latency, and L_rule records which; in both replays it was the widening. It is measured on a one-minute grid, so the latency is always a multiple of 60 s, and onset is searched from 15 minutes before the shock's formation start up to its peak. A longer latency means the wallet left its quote in place longer.
  • Exp10's four absorption stories. Closer: the wallet's own best hit-side quote at onset is at or inside the peer median distance. Slow to pull: its reaction latency is at or above the peer median. Size: its resting hit-side size at onset is at least three times the peer median. Run through: it was filled on quotes that had been resting a long time, read off the resting-age distribution rather than from a threshold. §6.4 argues for a fifth, for a wallet that is none of the four because it kept replacing a large quote near the best price during the move.
  • Peer median. In the replays, the median over every other MM holding a resting quote in that window. These MMs differ in size, so the comparison is against all MMs, not against MMs of similar size (§9).

Statistics

  • Quantiles. A cell with three numbers is p25 / p50 / p75; where a fuller picture matters the source CSV also carries p5 and p95. A share row is a single proportion, not a quantile.
  • Spearman rho. Rank correlation, so it measures monotone association and is unaffected by the log scales these variables need. It is descriptive here and identifies nothing causal.
  • Recall, lift, Jaccard. Recall is the share of the 181 roster shocks whose formation window overlaps an event of a rule. Lift is recall divided by the recall of a rule that flags the same number of bins at random. Bin Jaccard is bins flagged by both of two rules over bins flagged by either, as in §3.4.

Event definitions

Every number on this page is measured on one of five event sets. Three are selected on market-wide taker flow and two on a wallet's own inventory, and each set marks start, peak and end on its own clock. A shaded note under every section heading names the set and the count that section uses.

An episode is a group of set-4 shocks that overlap in time. Sets 4 and 5 carry 5-minute bin labels, and the clock time is the label plus five minutes (§15). Two further families sit beside set 3 in §9: F2 is the 399 of the 478 two-sided windows with |I| < 1/3 at the peak bin, and F3 is the 327 F1 events that set 1 never selects.

The 1-minute run (sets 2 and 3)

  • Run. Nt is in-direction net taker USD in minute t, and p95 is the 95th percentile of N over the 6 hours before the window. The run is the set of minutes with Nt > 0.25 × p95, with gaps of up to 3 minutes merged, and it qualifies when some minute reaches Nt ≥ 3 × p95. ts is its first minute and te its last.
  • Where the search looks. The minutes searched are those of the duration run: the stretch of qualifying 5-minute bins around the event's half hour, with one non-qualifying bin allowed inside. 5-minute bins are used only there: they never select an event and never set its start or end.
  • How a run ends. Flip: the minute after te has N ≤ 0, so the opposite side took over; 74.0% of F1 runs. Fade: N stays positive but falls below the 0.25 × p95 exit threshold; 19.7%. Edge: the search window ends; 6.3%.

Wallet-level definitions

  • Shocked wallet-event (set 1). An active MM with |q(t1) − q(t0)| ≥ 3 sig24 over the event window, where q is the exchange-reported HYPE position and sig24 the wallet's own 24-hour position scale in HYPE (§4.1). This is the end rule. §8 compares it with the peak rule, maxt0≤t≤t1 |q(t) − q(t0)| ≥ 3 sig24.
  • Own peak. The minute of the wallet's largest signed excursion from q(t0) inside the box. The accumulation phase (ACC) runs from t0 to the own peak and the unwind phase (UNW) from the own peak to two hours after it, so two MMs in one event have different phase boundaries.
  • Recovery (sets 4 and 5). T60 is the minutes after the peak until 60% of the peak deviation is given back. If that has not happened within 360 minutes, T60 is recorded as more than 360 minutes. §10 and §13 read the bin labels as clock times, so their windows sit five minutes early; §6, §7, §11 and §14 use clock times.

How the definition changed

  1. 2026-09-05, net-flow events (set 1). Events are 30-minute bins where net taker USD has |zNET| ≥ 3.70, the top 5%, giving 915 events. 5-minute bins were tested and rejected: they fire 9 to 25 times a day, and the buy/sell ratio rule at 5 minutes finds roster shocks at the rate of random flags (lift 1.0). Each event's window is its 30-minute box.
  2. 2026-09-08, 1-minute anchors for the same 915 (set 2). Start and end come from a run of in-direction net flow per minute, using the 3 × and 0.25 × p95 thresholds. This changed the clock and kept the same events. The population rerun of that date measured the 30-minute boxes again, so every population result on this page is on set 1.
  3. 2026-09-10, side-surge families (set 3). Selection stays on 30-minute bins, but each side gets its own z. One side must surge (z ≥ 3.81 buy, 3.89 sell) and dominate the bin, and the cutoff was tuned so the count, 922, matches the 915. The 1-minute runs reuse the 2026-09-08 construction.
  4. 2026-09-15, the population build on F1 (set 3). The §4 measurements were run on the 922 side surges twice, on their 1-minute runs and on their 30-minute windows. The shocked share of event × MM pairs is 5.2% on the runs and 5.3% on the windows against 5.9% on set 1, and the half hours set 1 never selects shock MMs at about half that rate (§9.7).

Event set per finding

  • Set 1, 915 events (914 in §4.4, §8 and §12): absorption, shocked MMs, controls and equity (§4); the 25,705 event × MM pairs that built at least one own position scale of inventory, and their early or late unwind (§4.4); shock-rate predictors (§5.4); the 168 bps price cutoff and the classes (§3); peers on the other side of the unwind in 45% of events with a shocked MM (§4.8); biggest absorbers against flagged wallets (§8); quoting while unwinding, 7,492 shocked event × MM pairs (§12).
  • Set 3: the 327 half hours the net rule never selects, the 14-minute median run and the 74.0% flip share (§9), and the shocked-against-unshocked statistics on its own windows (§9.7).
  • Set 4: recall of the price-first and flow-first triggers (§3.4), the quote response of a shocked roster MM (§10), and the three replays: episode 89 (§6), episode 100 (§7), and episodes 39 and 47, where $1m to $9m single taker orders carry the surge (§13, §14).
  • Set 5: recovery speed as a trait of the MM, 812 shocks (§11).

1. Changes from the earlier definition

Earlier and new definition, axis by axis

A shock definition has three axes. The size hyperparameter sets how large a move must be. The trigger is either a single MM's inventory or market-level taker imbalance. The interaction with price and equity decides whether a shock mattered.

AxisEarlier Exp8 definitionThis reportWhere
TriggerPer-MM inventory deviation, z at or above 6 against its own trailing scale, on the roster tenMarket net taker flow, chosen from three measures and compared with a price trigger; every active MM measured around events and matched controls§3, §4
Size hyperparameterOne cutoff (|z| at or above 6, $100k floor) with a sensitivity tableThree cutoffs at two bin sizes, scored on count, class mix, recall of the 181 roster shocks and lift; a stricter subset of the same events§3
Price and equity interactionShock atlas: price z in the formation bin, equity at snapshotsEvent classes by price move and liquidations; equity, closed PnL and BTC, ETH and SOL moves for every active MM; two tick replays that order price and flow by the second§3, §4, §6, §7

2. Literature on order imbalance

Published extreme-event studies define the event on price, with a far tighter cutoff than the ones considered here. §3.4 builds that price definition on HYPE and compares it with the net-flow trigger. Four points from sixteen verified references carry over to HYPE.

Four precedents
  • The ratio form is the equity standard, for one stated reason.
    Chordia and Subrahmanyam (2004) scale imbalance by total trades or total dollars "to eliminate the impact of total trading activity". Chordia, Roll and Subrahmanyam (2008) use 5-minute clock bins because shorter bins worsen buy/sell classification error. Our data carry the aggressor flag, so that reason does not apply here.
  • Extreme-event papers define the event on the price, with a percentile, and a tight one.
    Brogaard, Carrion, Moyaert, Riordan, Shkilko and Sokolov (2018) define an extreme price movement as the 99.9th percentile of the absolute 10-second midquote return per stock, report results across a range of percentiles, and note that the 99.9th percentile of trade imbalance selects almost the same sample. The cutoffs considered here (a |z| of 3 or more, top 10%, top 5%) are two orders of magnitude looser. §3.4 builds this definition on HYPE 5-minute bins and compares it with the flow-first rule.
  • The precedents support local normalization, but not our exact estimator.
    Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov (2014) and Cont, Cucuringu and Zhang (2023) estimate or depth-scale within short windows; Comerton-Forde et al. (2010) use a trailing benchmark; Easley, O'Hara, Yang and Zhang (2024) use rolling lookbacks. Like these papers, we scale by a local trailing window. Unlike them, we use the median and MAD (median absolute deviation) of the seven days strictly before the bin, with a dollar floor, where they use a mean and standard deviation. We then apply a full-sample 95th-percentile cutoff, which none of them does, so our event count is in-sample.
  • Crypto perpetuals reverse one equity result.
    Silantyev (2019) finds trade-flow imbalance beats book-based order-flow imbalance on the BitMEX perpetual, naming thin depth and slow quote updates. That supports taker-side imbalance as the primary measure here and warns against importing an equity threshold.
Two methods to separate price-driven from flow-driven events

The reversal rule (more than two thirds reversed by a fixed horizon is transitory; Brogaard et al. 2018) and the state-space split of permanent (surprise order flow) from transitory (inventory) price pressure (Hendershott and Menkveld 2014). The tick replays in §6 and §7 answer the ordering question for two events directly instead.

Some items are verified to record and abstract only: the Chordia, Roll and Subrahmanyam (2002) methodology, Hasbrouck (1991), details of Menkveld and Yueshen (2019) and of Silantyev (2019), and the published venue of Easley, O'Hara, Yang and Zhang. No peer-reviewed Hyperliquid paper on order imbalance or liquidation cascades was found. One unrefereed 2026 preprint exists and is flagged as such.

3. The market flow trigger

Event set 1: 915 net-flow events on 30-minute boxes. Start t0 and end t1 are the open of the first and the close of the last flagged bin; the peak is the bin with the largest |zNET| (standardized net taker USD). Rules are scored against the 181 roster wallet shocks (set 4), and §3.4 builds 959 price-trigger events on the same half-hour bins.
Terms used here: Event window, Roster
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • Roster: the ten named HYPE MMs, MM01 to MM10, of the earlier per-wallet shock study.

A market event is a run of half hours in which HYPE net taker USD was extreme against the previous week. Net dollars select events better than the buy/sell ratio, and half-hour bins better than shorter ones. Each event is then classed by its price move and its share of liquidation flow. An alternative rule, built on a surge in one taker side rather than on net flow, is in §9.

Data
  • Data. Every HYPE taker fill, 2025-03-27 to 2026-06-30 UTC: 132,333 five-minute bins and 22,058 thirty-minute bins with trades, 461 dates (132,768 and 22,128 bins on the full grid; 131,486 and 21,923 have both a price and a valid zNET, §3.4).

3.1 Definitions

Measures, events, classes, scoring

Measures per bin t (Bt, St = taker buy and sell USD in the bin)

  • Net taker flow NETt=Bt−St, in USD. The measure the catalogue is built on.
  • Imbalance ratio IMBt=(Bt−St)/(Bt+St), in [−1,1]. The equity-literature form (§2); tested and rejected below.
  • Standardized measure zX,t=Xt−med7d(X)max(1.4826 MAD7d(X), floor) for X∈{NET,IMB}: median and MAD over the seven days of bins strictly before t. This is Exp8's inventory recipe with net taker flow in place of one wallet's deviation.
Why 7 days and these floors

The literature never standardizes by a full-sample sigma; every precedent is local (§2). Seven days is Exp8's window, so the two catalogues are comparable. The floors exist only to stop a division by a near-zero MAD in a dead week; the trailing robust sigma of net taker USD never falls below $87,564 at 5 minutes or $403,788 at 30 minutes, so the $25,000 floor removes 0 of 16,046 flags. A $250,000 floor would remove 14% of flags, so it would act as a size filter.

From flagged bins to events

  • Flagged bin: |zNET,t| at or above the cutoff. The recommended cutoff is 3.70, the top 5% of all 30-minute bins.
  • Event: a maximal run of flagged bins whose NETt has the same sign, allowing one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. One flagged bin is enough to make an event; 84% (767) of the 915 events are exactly one 30-minute bin, the longest is 180 minutes. The peak bin is the one with the largest |zNET|.
  • Hit side: the side the takers traded on (buy when NET>0). MMs absorb on the opposite side, so their inventory moves against the flow. The MM side that absorbs the takers (asks when takers buy) is the absorption side, written SAME in tables; the other side is the exit side, written OPP. These two labels are used for every fill and every resting order in §4.
  • One-sided event: the hit side's taker USD per bin is at least 1.5 times its median per-bin rate over the six hours before the event, and at least twice the same ratio for the other side. Otherwise two-sided (both sides surged, or neither did). This is Exp8's rule.
Why these one-sided constants

The two constants are Exp8's, kept so the label means the same thing in both catalogues. The first says the hit side really surged (half again its normal rate); the second says the surge was not matched on the other side. Longer bins give fewer one-sided events, because a half hour is long enough for flow to come back: 91.1% at 5 minutes, 54.5% at 30 minutes, and 64.1% in the earlier study, whose formation windows are 25 minutes at the median. Quote the label with its bin size.

Three classes, decided in this order

  • Liquidation cascade: forced taker USD (liquidations plus ADL) is at least 10% of the event's taker USD. 41 of 915 events.
  • Big price move: the start-to-end mid move is at least 168 bps in absolute value. 168 bps is the 95th percentile of |return| over all 22,128 thirty-minute bins of the fifteen months, so big means in the top 5% of all half hours in the sample. 353 of 915 events.
  • No big price move: everything else. 521 events.
Why these class cutoffs

Forced share. At 5% the cascade share is 10.1% of events, at 10% it is 4.5%, at 25% 0.9%; the median event has a forced share of 0.001. Ten percent keeps the class small without emptying it.

Price gate. A relative gate, maxt|price zt|≥3 with price zt=returnt/(1.4826 med7d|return|), compares each bin with its own trailing week. It misclassifies moves that were large in dollars but happened in a volatile week: 2026-06-04 06:00 fell $72.54 to $67.80 (654 bps) and is "no big move" under it. The absolute gate uses the overall distribution instead: p90 = 129 bps, p95 = 168, p99 = 271, p99.9 = 715. Under p95, 163 of 915 events change class: 139 no-big-move events become big, 24 big events become no-big-move. The big-move share is 53.6% at p90, 38.6% at p95, 15.2% at p99; p95 keeps the class at a third of the sample. The relative flag is kept as a column (big_price_move) for anyone who wants "big for the week".

Scoring a rule

  • Recall: the share of the 181 Exp8 roster-MM inventory shocks whose formation window ([form start,peak+5 min)) overlaps an event of the rule.
  • Lift: recall divided by the recall a rule flagging the same number of bins at random would reach. Lift 1 means the rule finds roster shocks no better than chance.
  • With roster shock: the share of the rule's events that contain at least one roster shock.

3.2 Which rule

  • Recall, lift: recall is the share of the 181 roster shocks that fall inside a rule's events; lift is how many times more often a flagged bin holds a roster shock than a random bin.
  • Event classes: liquidation cascade: forced flow at least 10% of taker USD; otherwise big price move: the mid moved at least 168 bps from start to end, the top 5% of all half hours; otherwise no big price move.
  • One-sided, two-sided: an event is one-sided when the hit side's taker USD surges and the other side's does not; two-sided when both surge.
Terms used here: Event window, sig24, Roster, Recall, lift, Event classes, One-sided, two-sided
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • sig24: the MM's own position scale, in HYPE, recomputed for each event from its positions over the 24 hours before t0. It is the largest of three numbers: 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the position from its trailing 6-hour median, 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position, and $12,500 of HYPE at the t0 mid.
  • Roster: the ten named HYPE MMs, MM01 to MM10, of the earlier per-wallet shock study.
  • Recall, lift: recall is the share of the 181 roster shocks that fall inside a rule's events; lift is how many times more often a flagged bin holds a roster shock than a random bin.
  • Event classes: liquidation cascade: forced flow at least 10% of taker USD; otherwise big price move: the mid moved at least 168 bps from start to end, the top 5% of all half hours; otherwise no big price move.
  • One-sided, two-sided: an event is one-sided when the hit side's taker USD surges and the other side's does not; two-sided when both surge.

  • Net dollars, not the buy/sell ratio.
    Flagging the same share of bins, the ratio rule's events hold about a quarter of the dollars, and its lift is far lower. A half hour can be 95% buys and 5% sells while holding almost no dollars, because a ratio carries no size. The standardized ratio cannot reach a z of three at all: it is bounded, and its trailing median absolute deviation (MAD) is about 0.29.
  • 30-minute bins, not 5-minute.
    At 5 minutes the same rules fire 9 to 25 times a day (Table 2); at 30 minutes, 2 to 4 times a day.
  • Top 5% for the net-flow events; z of 6 or more as a stricter subset.
    A tighter cutoff keeps a subset of the same events, so it changes the count and the class mix but not what an event is. The top 5% is used where sample size matters (§4); the 300 events at z of 6 or more all lie inside it.

3.3 Event classes

Terms used here: Event window, Shocked, Forced, voluntary flow, Roster, Event classes, One-sided, two-sided, rho
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Forced, voluntary flow: forced flow is taker USD from liquidations and auto-deleveraging (ADL); voluntary flow is all other taker USD. A victim is the wallet that was force-closed.
  • Roster: the ten named HYPE MMs, MM01 to MM10, of the earlier per-wallet shock study.
  • Event classes: liquidation cascade: forced flow at least 10% of taker USD; otherwise big price move: the mid moved at least 168 bps from start to end, the top 5% of all half hours; otherwise no big price move.
  • One-sided, two-sided: an event is one-sided when the hit side's taker USD surges and the other side's does not; two-sided when both surge.
  • rho: Spearman rank correlation, from −1 to +1; p tests rho = 0.

  • Liquidations are a small part of event flow.
    41 of 915 events are cascades, and in the median event forced flow is a share of 0.001.
  • Among big price moves, a two-sided event carries 70% more dollars for a move only 13% larger.
    The extra volume may be MMs trading with each other rather than new one-way pressure. Taker flow alone cannot test this; the counterparty split in §4 can.
  • In 97.7% of events the start-to-end price move has the sign of the net taker flow.
    This does not say which came first. Two events are ordered second by second on tick data in §6 and §7.
  • Roster shocks sit in the big-move and cascade cells
    , at 1.1 to 5.9 times their rate in the no-big-move cell of the same sidedness.
Class counts under the weekly-relative gate

Under the relative gate (max|price z|≥3) the cells are big price move 120 + 118, cascade 12 + 29 and no big move 367 + 269. Crossing the two gates: 214 events are big under both, 24 big only under the relative gate, 139 big only under the absolute gate and 497 not big under either. The 41 cascades are the same under both, because the cascade test is applied first.

  • Among these events, more one-sided flow goes with a smaller price move.
    The absolute buy/sell ratio over the whole event, |buys − sells| / (buys + sells), and |move| correlate −0.23 at 5 minutes and −0.30 at 30 minutes, and stay negative inside a single flow direction. Standardized net dollar flow correlates +0.38 and +0.39 on the same events (Figure 2). Every event here already passed the top-5% net-flow cutoff, so this holds for selected events only.
Relative price gate

The primary gate above is absolute: a big move is at least 168 bps, the p95 of all half-hours in the sample. The alternative calls a move big when its price z reached 3, meaning big relative to that week. Both flags are carried in the catalogue, so either can be quoted; only the label changes, never the event times.

  • The two gates disagree on 17.8% of events.
    The weekly-relative gate gives 238 big-price events, 41 liquidation cascades and 636 no-big-move; the absolute gate gives 353, 41 and 521. The 163 events that move between classes are all non-cascade.
  • The disagreement runs one way, and that is why the absolute gate is primary.
    A relative gate rescales itself in a volatile week, so a large move inside a volatile week fails it. 2026-06-04 06:00 fell 654 bps and the weekly-relative gate calls it no-big-move, because that week was volatile enough for 654 bps to be ordinary.
  • Nothing downstream depends on the choice.
    The population results in §4 are measured per event and pooled over all 915, 2025-10-10 included (§4.4 pools 914); the gate enters only where a table is split by price class.

3.4 Price trigger against flow trigger

Terms used here: Event window, Roster, Recall, lift, Event classes, One-sided, two-sided
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • Roster: the ten named HYPE MMs, MM01 to MM10, of the earlier per-wallet shock study.
  • Recall, lift: recall is the share of the 181 roster shocks that fall inside a rule's events; lift is how many times more often a flagged bin holds a roster shock than a random bin.
  • Event classes: liquidation cascade: forced flow at least 10% of taker USD; otherwise big price move: the mid moved at least 168 bps from start to end, the top 5% of all half hours; otherwise no big price move.
  • One-sided, two-sided: an event is one-sided when the hit side's taker USD surges and the other side's does not; two-sided when both surge.

On HYPE, about a third of the flow trigger's half hours are also flagged by a price trigger. The rule used here is flow-first: it flags half hours on net taker USD. The literature's extreme-event definition is price-first: Brogaard, Carrion, Moyaert, Riordan, Shkilko and Sokolov (2018) call an extreme price movement any 10-second interval whose absolute midquote return is in the top 0.1% for that stock, and report that the top 0.1% of trade imbalances picks almost the same intervals. Each price rule below flags exactly as many bins as the flow rule it is compared with, on the same bins, so the overlap of the two rules compares like with like.

How the rules are matched

Matched pairs, per grid (5-minute or 30-minute bins) and quantile q∈{90,95,99,99.9}

  • Price rule Pq: |returnt| at or above its overall q-th percentile (30-minute: 129 / 168 / 271 / 718 bps over the 21,923 bins with a price and a valid zNET, 715 bps at p99.9 over all 22,128 bins; 5-minute: 54 / 70 / 115 / 215 bps).
  • Volatility-scaled price rule PZq: |price zt| at or above its own q-th percentile, where price zt=returnt/(1.4826 med7d|return|).
  • Flow rule Fq: |zNET,t| at or above its overall q-th percentile. F95 on 30-minute bins is the recommended rule (915 events).
  • Universe: bins with both a price and a valid zNET: 21,923 at 30 minutes, 131,486 at 5 minutes. Flagged counts are identical within a pair (no ties broke the match).
  • Overlap: bin Jaccard = bins flagged by both over bins flagged by either; the chance level for two unrelated rules at the same selectivity is q'/(2−q') with q'=1−q/100, so 0.026 at q=95. Events are built from each rule's flagged bins with the §3.1 grouping rule; event overlap is the share of one rule's events that overlap in time with an event of the other.

  • The two triggers share about a third of their half hours.
    34% of the flow rule's half hours are also extreme-return half hours, and 38% of its events overlap a price event. The bin overlap (Jaccard: bins flagged by both over bins flagged by either) is eight times what two unrelated rules would give. Scaling the return by the trailing week's volatility raises the shared share to 43% of bins. Agreement falls as the cutoff tightens, to a Jaccard of 0.02 at the 99.9th percentile.
  • The flow rule finds more roster shocks at every matched selectivity
    , recalling 57.5% of the 181 against 30.9% for the price rule at the recommended point, and 80.7% against 58.6% at 5 minutes.
  • Price-rule events also differ in kind.
    Price-first events are two-sided 1.5 times as often (70% against 45%) and almost all clear the big-move gate by construction; flow-first events are bigger in dollars and only 39% move the price 168 bps. Brogaard et al.'s near-equivalence of the two on equities does not hold on HYPE at these quantiles.

At the 99.9th percentile on 5-minute bins, the literature's own rule, 20% of the flow bins are also price bins, so the near-coincidence the paper reports for equities does not appear on HYPE. That price rule gives 124 events over fifteen months (0.27 per day), 66% one-sided, 15% cascades and 6.6% recall of the roster shocks.

Data holes and 2025-10-10

Holes were found by hand: 435 five-minute bins with no taker fills (236 on 2025-11-24, 180 on 2026-04-23) and 40 bins with a null mid at 00:00. No recommended-rule event falls on the two hole days; two events touch a null-mid bin and carry a flag. 2025-10-10 gives five events including the sample maximum (21:00 to 21:30, peak |z| 156.5, $829m of taker USD, 35% forced, four roster shocks inside); it is excluded from every pooled statistic in §4 (910 events) except §4.4, which keeps it (914 events).

4. Active HYPE MMs in events and controls

Event set 1: the 915 net-flow events on 30-minute bins, each with one control window at the same clock time. Pooled statistics use all 915 events, 2025-10-10 included. There are 120,269 rows, one per event and active MM, every date included (126,978 under the fill-based gate). Each event window runs from t0, the open of its first flagged bin, to t1, the close of its last. §4.4 reads the 25,705 rows whose inventory grew by at least one own sigma, the MM’s own position scale, on the absorption side.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC: order types: ALO is post-only (rejected if it would cross), IOC is immediate-or-cancel, GTC rests until cancelled.
Terms used here: Event window, HYPE MM, Active MM, sig24, Shocked, Absorption side, exit side, Control window, Markout M30, M60, M120, ALO, IOC, GTC
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • HYPE MM: a wallet the project's daily label model (v5d) classes as a HYPE market maker on that date. The label is per date.
  • Active MM: a labelled HYPE MM with at least one post-only (ALO) fill in the 2 hours before the event and at least one fill inside it.
  • sig24: the MM's own position scale, in HYPE, recomputed for each event from its positions over the 24 hours before t0. It is the largest of three numbers: 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the position from its trailing 6-hour median, 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position, and $12,500 of HYPE at the t0 mid.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Absorption side, exit side: the absorption side is the maker side the event's takers trade against (the bid when takers sell, the ask when takers buy); an MM filled there builds a position against the flow. The exit (opposite) side is the other one.
  • Control window: for each event, the same UTC clock time and length on the nearest date (+1, −1, +2, −2, … days) with no event in the window or within 2 hours of it. Controls are not matched on volume or volatility.
  • Markout M30, M60, M120: what a fill is worth against the mid 30, 60 or 120 minutes later, in bps of the fill's USD; positive is favourable to the wallet.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC: order types: ALO is post-only (rejected if it would cross), IOC is immediate-or-cancel, GTC rests until cancelled.

Every active HYPE MM is measured in each of the 915 events of the §3 catalogue and in that event’s control window. The wallets that absorb the flow without being shocked are in §8.

  • The events are the net-flow trigger of §3.
    A 30-minute bin is flagged when its robust net-taker-flow score is in the top 5% of all bins, at or above 3.70.
  • 87.0% of shocked MMs moved inventory against the taker flow.
    Of 7,193 shocked wallet-events, 6,257 moved against the net taker flow (shorter when takers bought) and 936 moved with it. In 37 of the 852 events with a shocked MM, every shocked MM moved with the flow.
Sample and grain
  • Sample. 915 event windows and 915 matched controls; pooled statistics use every date, 2025-10-10 included (915 events). The event classes are the absolute price gate classes of §3.3.
  • Grain. One row per window and active MM. PRE2H, PRE30, the event and POST are measured separately: the 2 hours before, the half hour before, the event itself and the 2 hours after.

4.1 Definitions

  • Covered row: a row for which at least half of the orders behind the MM's pre-event post-only fills are found in the order store.
Terms used here: Active MM, Shocked, Absorption side, exit side, PRE2H, PRE30, POST, ALO, IOC, GTC, Covered row
  • Active MM: a labelled HYPE MM with at least one post-only (ALO) fill in the 2 hours before the event and at least one fill inside it.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Absorption side, exit side: the absorption side is the maker side the event's takers trade against (the bid when takers sell, the ask when takers buy); an MM filled there builds a position against the flow. The exit (opposite) side is the other one.
  • PRE2H, PRE30, POST: PRE2H is the 2 hours ending at t0; PRE30 the last 30 minutes before t0; POST the 2 hours after t1.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC: order types: ALO is post-only (rejected if it would cross), IOC is immediate-or-cancel, GTC rests until cancelled.
  • Covered row: a row for which at least half of the orders behind the MM's pre-event post-only fills are found in the order store.
Full definitions

Windows, population, controls

  • Event window. The catalogue event's own span [t0,t1) from §3.1: one 30-minute bin for 84% of events, up to 180 minutes. Four windows are measured separately. PRE2H is the two hours ending at t0, PRE30 the last 30 minutes before t0, EV the event itself [t0,t1), and POST the two hours beginning at t1. The reversion tail runs to t1+6 h.
  • Active MM. A wallet the project’s daily label model (v5d) calls a HYPE market maker on that date that, in PRE2H, has at least one ALO (post-only) fill, and has at least one fill during the event. On the dates where the fill table carries no order-type (time-in-force) value at all (2026-04-16 to 2026-04-22), the ALO test falls back to at least one maker fill in PRE2H. Which MMs this removes is in Table 6.
  • Matched control. The same UTC clock time and length on the nearest date, trying +1, −1, +2, −2, … days away, with no catalogue event in the window or in the two hours either side. 527 controls are one day later, 218 are one day earlier, 92 are two days later, 50 are two days earlier and 28 are 3 to 6 days away. Controls are not matched on volume or volatility, so part of any event-minus-control gap may simply be a busier market.
  • Grain. One row per window × active MM. An event's 136 active MMs are 136 rows. Quantiles "over window × MM rows" treat every MM in every window as one observation. Quantiles "across windows" first compute one number per window.

Inventory and its own scale

  • Position and inventory change. qt is the exchange-reported HYPE position, rebuilt from the wallet’s fills in block order. The event inventory change is dq=qt1−qt0, in HYPE, signed: negative means the wallet ended the window shorter than it began it.
  • Own scale sig24. sig24=max[1.4826 MAD(q−median6hq), 0.02 p95|q|, 12500/mid], with every term computed over the 24 hours before the event. It is the largest of three quantities: the wallet's robust deviation from its trailing 6-hour median position; 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position; and the HYPE worth $12,500 at the mid at t0. The last two are floors. A shock needs |dq|≥3 sig24, so every shock is an inventory change of at least $37,500 at the start mid and at least 6% of the wallet's 95th-percentile absolute position.
  • Shocked. |zdq|=|dq|/sig24≥3. It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Unshocked. An active MM in the same window that is not shocked.
  • Order-store coverage. A row is covered when at least half of the orders behind its PRE2H ALO fills appear in the order store. Resting-book, message-rate and order-count values exist only for covered rows; on an uncovered row they are missing, not zero. 100.0% of shocked, 99.9% of unshocked and 99.9% of control rows are covered under the any-fill rule.

Absorption and concentration

  • Absorption side and opposite side. The absorption side is the side takers traded on (the ask when net taker flow is buying). MMs absorb on that side, so their inventory moves against the flow. The opposite side is the other side. Resting-order rows are averages of one-minute snapshots, not counts of events.
  • Absorption. For one wallet, its maker USD on the absorption side divided by all taker USD on that side. For a two-sided event the denominator still uses the single net-flow absorption side only, not both directions pooled.
  • Absorber. An active MM whose absorption-side maker USD is positive. The absorbers column counts how many MMs filled any taker flow on that side, whatever the amount.
  • Absorption rank. Position in the descending order of absorption-side maker USD among the window's active MMs. Rank 1 is the largest absorber during the event, not the largest MM beforehand.
  • Effective N, and what 1/HHI means. Let si be wallet i's share of labelled-MM absorption-side maker USD, over the MMs with si>0. The Herfindahl index is HHI=∑isi2 and effective N is 1/HHI. Effective N is the number of equally sized absorbers that would be as concentrated as the event was. The median event has 115 MMs with some absorption-side volume but an effective N of 15.49: most of them fill very little.
  • Top-5 share. The sum of the five largest si.
  • Concentration C. C=maxi|dqi|/∑i|dqi|, over the window's active MMs: the largest single wallet's share of the event's total absolute inventory change. C=1 means one MM carried all of it; C=1/n means all n carried equally. It is an event-level number, not a per-wallet one. C stays below 0.6 in every event. §17.1 proposes 0.6 as the level at which an event is one MM's own problem.
  • Direction agreement D. D=|∑idqi|/∑i|dqi|, net over gross, again over active MMs. D=1 means every MM's inventory moved the same way, so the population as a whole took on a one-directional position; D=0 means the changes cancel exactly, so the population's net change is zero. D is what separates one-sided from two-sided events; C does not.

Timing landmarks

  • Own peak minute, flow peak minute and price extreme minute are minute indices on a one-minute grid with minute 0 at t0. Let s=sign(dq) and define the wallet's signed excursion at minute t as s·(qt−qt0), so a wallet building a short position has a rising excursion.
  • Own peak minute (end direction) is the minute maximizing that excursion; peak excursion is the maximum itself, in HYPE, or divided by sig24 when quoted in sigma.
  • Flow peak minute is the minute with the largest absorption-side taker USD. Price extreme minute is the minute of the lowest mid inside the event window if the event's price move is negative, of the highest if positive.
  • Baseline is the median absorption-side taker USD per minute over PRE2H, one number per event.

Early and late unwinders

  • Absorption-side sign and built inventory. s=+1 when takers sell, so absorbing them makes the MM longer, and s=−1 when takers buy. The inventory built since the window start is xt=s (qt−qt0) in HYPE, read at the end of each 1-minute bin. It is positive when the position has moved toward the absorption side.
  • Accumulation A and own absorption-side peak t*. A is the largest xt over the minutes of the window, and t* is the first minute attaining it. A is reported in HYPE, in USD at the mid of the peak minute, and divided by sig24. The class rule below uses the HYPE value.
  • Level at the peak L. L=s (qt*−median6h q), where the median is over the six hours before t0. L is how far the peak position sits on the absorption side of that six-hour median.
  • Absorber that accumulated inventory. An active MM in one event with all three of: A≥sig24; L≥sig24; and absorption-side maker fills larger than all opposite-side fills over [t0,t*), both in HYPE. The last condition means the inventory was built by filling takers, not by the wallet's own crossing orders.
  • ACC and UNW for these absorbers. ACC is [t0,t*) and UNW is [t*,t*+2 h). Both are anchored on the absorption-side peak, not on the end-direction own peak used for shocked MMs (Phases and markouts, below).
  • Price extreme text. The minute of the highest 1-minute mid over [t0,t1+30 min) when the event's price move is up, and of the lowest when it is down.
  • Given back at the price extreme. G=1−xtextA, with x read at the end of the extreme minute. G=0.5 means half of A is gone. A negative G means the wallet held more than A by then.
  • Early unwinder. An absorber that accumulated inventory with t*≤text and G≥0.5.
  • Late unwinder. Every other absorber that accumulated inventory. Late unwinders split in two: late, held more than half, with own peak at or before the price extreme and G under 0.5, and late, peak after the price extreme, with own peak after it. Early and late partition the absorbers that accumulated inventory.
  • Minutes to half. Minutes from t* to the first minute with xt≤A/2. The search stops at 360 minutes. A value of 360 means the MM had not unwound half its accumulation by then, so the true time is longer.

Phases and markouts

  • ACC and UNW. ACC is accumulation, from t0 to the wallet's own peak minute (end direction); UNW is unwind, from that minute to two hours after it. Each MM has its own peak, so its two phases start and end at its own times.
  • ACC submits / PRE2H and UNW submits / PRE2H are that phase's order submissions per minute divided by the same wallet's submissions per minute in PRE2H. A value of 1.37 means it submitted 37% more orders per minute while accumulating than it had in the two prior hours.
  • Taker share of a phase is crossing (taker) fill USD divided by all fill USD in that phase, for that wallet.
  • Markout Mk. For one fill at price p, size v, with d=+1 for a buy and −1 for a sell, Mk=d (midt+k−p) v in dollars: what the fill is worth marked to the mid k minutes later. A group of fills is reported in bps as 104∑jMk,j/∑jpjvj, signed so that positive is favourable to the wallet. k is 30, 60 or 120 minutes. Event maker M30 is that quantity over the wallet's non-crossing fills inside the event window, at k=30.

Equity and closed PnL

  • Equity is the whole account across all coins, read from account-state snapshots whose cadence is 2 to 5.5 hours. A change is measured against the last snapshot in the 24 hours before t0. Because snapshots are hours apart, the event-end value spans somewhat more than the event, and fewer than half of wallet-events have a value at exactly +2 h.
  • Below −1% and below −5% are the shares of shocked wallet-events whose equity change is below those levels.
  • Own closed-PnL baseline. A wallet-event is flagged as unusually poor when its realized closed PnL falls below that wallet's own 10th percentile of closed PnL over the prior seven days. The flag marks an unusual outcome for that wallet; it does not show that the event caused a loss. It exists only for the 1,035 wallets in the dense panel (91% of active-MM rows).
  • Major-coin range. A window is counted as having a major-coin move when BTC, ETH or SOL also had a price range over the same clock window above the 90th percentile of its ranges over the full sample.

§4 compares groups. It does not estimate what an event causes.

  • Some rows under the any-fill rule are not market making. That rule asks for one fill of any kind in the two hours before the event and one during it. Under it, 6.9% of unshocked rows have no post-only (ALO) fill in those two hours and 6.0% have exactly one fill.

4.2 How many MMs absorb, and how many are shocked

  • Effective N, C, D: effective N is 1 over the sum of squared absorption shares: the number of equal absorbers that would be as concentrated.
Terms used here: HYPE MM, Active MM, sig24, Shocked, Absorption side, exit side, Control window, Forced, voluntary flow, Event classes, One-sided, two-sided, Effective N, C, D
  • HYPE MM: a wallet the project's daily label model (v5d) classes as a HYPE market maker on that date. The label is per date.
  • Active MM: a labelled HYPE MM with at least one post-only (ALO) fill in the 2 hours before the event and at least one fill inside it.
  • sig24: the MM's own position scale, in HYPE, recomputed for each event from its positions over the 24 hours before t0. It is the largest of three numbers: 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the position from its trailing 6-hour median, 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position, and $12,500 of HYPE at the t0 mid.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Absorption side, exit side: the absorption side is the maker side the event's takers trade against (the bid when takers sell, the ask when takers buy); an MM filled there builds a position against the flow. The exit (opposite) side is the other one.
  • Control window: for each event, the same UTC clock time and length on the nearest date (+1, −1, +2, −2, … days) with no event in the window or within 2 hours of it. Controls are not matched on volume or volatility.
  • Forced, voluntary flow: forced flow is taker USD from liquidations and auto-deleveraging (ADL); voluntary flow is all other taker USD. A victim is the wallet that was force-closed.
  • Event classes: liquidation cascade: forced flow at least 10% of taker USD; otherwise big price move: the mid moved at least 168 bps from start to end, the top 5% of all half hours; otherwise no big price move.
  • One-sided, two-sided: an event is one-sided when the hit side's taker USD surges and the other side's does not; two-sided when both surge.
  • Effective N, C, D: effective N is 1 over the sum of squared absorption shares: the number of equal absorbers that would be as concentrated. C is the largest MM's share of summed absolute inventory change. D is net over gross inventory change: 1 when every MM moved the same way.

4.3 MM state before the event

  • Absorber, absorption share: an absorber is an active MM with maker fills on the absorption side during the event.
Terms used here: sig24, Shocked, Absorption side, exit side, Absorber, absorption share, Control window, ALO, IOC, GTC, Submits, cancels
  • sig24: the MM's own position scale, in HYPE, recomputed for each event from its positions over the 24 hours before t0. It is the largest of three numbers: 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the position from its trailing 6-hour median, 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position, and $12,500 of HYPE at the t0 mid.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Absorption side, exit side: the absorption side is the maker side the event's takers trade against (the bid when takers sell, the ask when takers buy); an MM filled there builds a position against the flow. The exit (opposite) side is the other one.
  • Absorber, absorption share: an absorber is an active MM with maker fills on the absorption side during the event. Absorption rank orders them by that maker USD, 1 = largest.
  • Control window: for each event, the same UTC clock time and length on the nearest date (+1, −1, +2, −2, … days) with no event in the window or within 2 hours of it. Controls are not matched on volume or volatility.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC: order types: ALO is post-only (rejected if it would cross), IOC is immediate-or-cancel, GTC rests until cancelled.
  • Submits, cancels: new limit orders and cancels. The venue records a modify as one cancel plus one new order, so cancels per submit sits near 1.

Column key and source
Each cell is p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95 over window × MM rows, one quantile per line; every date, 2025-10-10 included. Shocked: an event row with |zdq| ≥ 3, 7,193 rows. Unshocked: an event row below that threshold, 113,076 rows. Control: a row for an MM active in the matched control window, 94,282 rows. A control window has the same UTC clock time and duration as its event, on the nearest date whose window and two-hour buffers hold no catalogue event. Controls are matched on clock time and length only, not on volume or volatility (§16). Absorption side is the maker side the event’s takers trade against, the side whose fills build the position; opposite side is the other; a control inherits the side of its event. A bin is 5 minutes. Order counts use covered rows only (§4.1). Event maker M30 is the 30-minute markout of the wallet’s maker fills in the event on that side, positive favourable. Column key and source
Each cell is p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95 over covered window × MM rows, one quantile per line: 7,193 shocked, 113,046 unshocked and 94,188 control rows. Resting orders, resting size, minutes with a quote, submits, submitted size, cancels and traded volume are averaged over every minute of the pre-event horizon, zero-quote minutes included. Mean size per resting order and the three distances are over minutes with at least one resting order on that side (6,561 shocked rows on the absorption side). Distances are bps from the mid at that minute, median over the horizon’s minutes: best-level is the nearest resting order, size-weighted weights every resting order by size, farthest is the outermost. p5 is negative on some distance rows because an order can rest inside the mid. Traded volume is filled USD on that side divided by the window length. Cancels per submit and opposite side share of submits are one number per row. One wallet’s two sides in the same window: each row first divides its absorption-side resting size by its opposite-side resting size, or subtracts its absorption-side best-level distance from its opposite-side one, and the cell quantiles those per-row numbers; a positive distance difference means the absorption-side best quote is nearer the mid. These rows use the rows with resting size on both sides (5,959 shocked, 88,038 unshocked and 76,154 control rows over the prior 2 h); the share row is one number per group, the share of those rows with more resting size on the absorption side. Source tables/pop_orderfixact_alldates/redef2_pop_order_placement_by_side.csv and tables/pop_orderfixact_alldates/review0917_pop_within_wallet_lean.csv.
  • Inside one wallet the resting size on the two sides is close to even.
    The median shocked row holds 1.01 times as much resting size on the absorption side as on the opposite side over the prior two hours (p25 0.95, p75 1.20) and 1.01 times over the prior 30 minutes. Dividing the median absorption-side size by the median opposite-side size across shocked rows gives 1.15 and 1.20, but those two medians belong to different wallets.
  • In control windows the two sides look alike.
    A control has no event, so the two sides it inherits should be interchangeable. The median per-row size ratio is 1.00 at both horizons, and 50.0% of rows hold more size on the absorption side. The median nearest absorption-side order sits 0.18 bps farther from the mid than the opposite-side one.
  • Shocked MMs also sent more orders to the absorption side.
    Over the prior 30 minutes the median shocked absorption-side submit rate is 1.14 times the median opposite-side rate. The median shocked row has a quote on the absorption side in 93.3% of minutes against 90.0% on the opposite side.
  • A per-row ratio removes size, not selection by the shock flag.
    At the median, shocked MMs rest 19 times the unshocked size on the absorption side, because only an MM resting a lot of size can move three of its own sigmas. Dividing a wallet’s two sides by each other removes that size difference. It does not remove selection: a wallet with more size resting on the side that gets hit is filled more there, so it is more likely to be shocked. A lean among shocked rows can then be a cause of the flag rather than a position taken ahead of the flow.

Remarks that need attention. Two readings of Table 9 that are not findings yet: each is a number without an explanation.

  • 55.6% of shocked rows hold more resting size on the absorption side over the prior two hours, against 48.8% of unshocked and 50.0% of control rows
    (54.7%, 46.7% and 48.5% over the prior 30 minutes). Needs attention: the shock flag is earned by fills on the absorption side, so a wallet that already rested more there is more likely to be flagged, and the gap may be selection by the flag rather than positioning ahead of the flow. Settled by comparing each shocked wallet-event with the same wallet’s unshocked event windows on the same hit side, or with unshocked rows matched on book size and prior-two-hour absorption-side size share.
  • Unshocked rows also quote their absorption side nearer the mid: a median per-row difference of +0.38 bps over the prior two hours and +0.79 over the prior 30 minutes, against +0.42 and +0.97 for shocked rows and −0.18 and −0.25 for controls.
    Needs attention: the side is assigned after the fact, from the flow that followed; if the mid was already drifting toward the side that was later hit, every resting quote on that side sits nearer the mid without any MM choosing it. Settled by measuring the same difference against the touch instead of the mid, and by splitting rows on the mid change over the prior two hours in the direction of the event’s flow.

4.4 Early and late unwinders among absorbers that accumulated inventory

Timing is measured only on MMs whose inventory actually grew on the absorption side during the event. 25,705 of the 126,846 event × active-MM rows clear that bar, a median 23 per event, and they hold 64% of all hit-side maker USD. Early means half of the accumulation was already gone when the price reached its extreme.

Section 4.4 has its own page with the other unwind results: early and late unwinders →

4.5 Aggressiveness of the unwind

Terms used here: Shocked, Control window, Taker share
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Control window: for each event, the same UTC clock time and length on the nearest date (+1, −1, +2, −2, … days) with no event in the window or within 2 hours of it. Controls are not matched on volume or volatility.
  • Taker share: the share of a wallet's fill USD in which its own order crossed the spread.

Shocked MMs unwind through limit orders, not by crossing the spread. 61.0% do not cross at all, and the median taker share of the unwind is 0.0%. Of those that crossed the spread at least sometimes before the event, 27.0% unwind with a taker share at least 1.2 times their pre-event share, against 22.8% of shocked rows in control windows.

4.6 Shocked against unshocked MMs, before and after

Terms used here: sig24, Shocked, Absorption side, exit side, PRE2H, PRE30, POST, Submits, cancels
  • sig24: the MM's own position scale, in HYPE, recomputed for each event from its positions over the 24 hours before t0. It is the largest of three numbers: 1.4826 times the median absolute deviation of the position from its trailing 6-hour median, 2% of its 95th-percentile absolute position, and $12,500 of HYPE at the t0 mid.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Absorption side, exit side: the absorption side is the maker side the event's takers trade against (the bid when takers sell, the ask when takers buy); an MM filled there builds a position against the flow. The exit (opposite) side is the other one.
  • PRE2H, PRE30, POST: PRE2H is the 2 hours ending at t0; PRE30 the last 30 minutes before t0; POST the 2 hours after t1.
  • Submits, cancels: new limit orders and cancels. The venue records a modify as one cancel plus one new order, so cancels per submit sits near 1.

4.7 Equity, closed PnL and cross-coin context

Terms used here: Event window, Shocked, Control window, Quantile cells
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones.   • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.
  • Control window: for each event, the same UTC clock time and length on the nearest date (+1, −1, +2, −2, … days) with no event in the window or within 2 hours of it. Controls are not matched on volume or volatility.
  • Quantile cells: a cell with five numbers is p5 / p25 / p50 / p75 / p95; with three, p25 / p50 / p75.

4.8 Counterparties of the unwind

Few of the shocked MMs’ unwind trades have another MM on the other side, and almost none have another shocked MM.

  • A median 14.4% of the shocked MMs’ unwind volume has a HYPE MM on the other side
    , and 0.41% a counterparty that was itself shocked in the same event. Measured on exact taker-maker pairs over the 528 events with a shocked MM and pair data, from 2025-09-27, when the pairing table starts, every date included.
  • The median event’s shocked MMs unwind $2.04m over the two hours after their peaks.
  • Peers take the other side of the aggregate unwind in 44.8% of the 857 events with a shocked MM, and in 49.4% of the 522 matched control windows with one.
    An event counts when the unshocked MMs’ net trade over the two hours after the window points the same way as the shocked MMs’ combined inventory change, so the unshocked MMs net-absorb the unwind. All three counterparty measures above use the fill-based gate (at least one fill in the two hours before the window and one inside it): 857 events with a shocked MM, every date, and 852 under the §4.1 rule.

5. Profile of all active HYPE MMs

Population: 148 MMs, one row per MM. §5.1 to §5.3 describe lifetime state. §5.4 counts how often each MM is shocked in the §4 events (set 1).
Terms used here: Event window, HYPE MM, Shocked
  • Event window: the day is cut into 30-minute bins that start at :00 and :30 UTC. A bin is flagged when HYPE net taker flow (taker buys minus taker sells, USD, all wallets) is far from normal: its distance from the median of the previous 7 days of bins, divided by a robust spread of those bins (1.4826 times their median absolute deviation, at least $25,000), is at least 3.70 in absolute value, the cutoff that keeps the top 5% of all bins in the sample. An event is a run of flagged bins of the same sign, with at most one unflagged bin between two flagged ones. Its window is [t0, t1): t0 is the open of the first flagged bin and t1 the close of the last, UTC clock times, the same for every MM in the event.
  • HYPE MM: a wallet the project's daily label model (v5d) classes as a HYPE market maker on that date. The label is per date.
  • Shocked: the MM's HYPE position changed from t0 to t1 by at least 3 sig24 (at least $37,500). It is decided per MM per event: the same MM can be shocked in one event and unshocked in the next.

Every qualifying HYPE MM is one equally weighted observation.

Population and grain
  • Population. 148 wallets labelled HYPE MM on at least 30 dates and active on at least 10 days. An active day has at least 300 grouped trades and $1 million of HYPE notional, from 2025-03-27 through 2026-06-30.
  • Grain. The profile table has one row per MM. Population quartiles are unweighted across MMs; a high-volume wallet does not count more.

5.1 Definitions

Variable definitions
  • Active 5-minute bin: a bin on an active day with at least one grouped fill row. Trades count those rows; volume is their USD notional.
  • Median signed position: the median exchange-reported HYPE position over active bins. It describes the level held half the time; negative is short. Share long is the share of active bins with positive position.
  • Inventory volatility: standard deviation of the 5-minute position change, in HYPE.
  • Deviation MAD: 1.4826×median|qt−median6h(q)|, in HYPE, where q is the MM's HYPE position. It is the typical distance from the MM's own recent inventory level.
  • Closed PnL per dollar: 104×∑jclosedPnLj/∑jVj, where Vj is fill USD, in bps.
  • Fill markout Mk. What a fill is worth against the mid k minutes later, in bps of the fill's USD; positive is favorable to the wallet. The rows below apply it over a wallet’s whole active history rather than inside an event window.
  • Volume-weighted M60 and M120: sum of fill markout dollars (positive is favorable) divided by the matching fill dollars, times 104, in bps.

5.2 Population distribution

Terms used here: Markout M30, M60, M120, ALO, IOC, GTC, Submits, cancels
  • Markout M30, M60, M120: what a fill is worth against the mid 30, 60 or 120 minutes later, in bps of the fill's USD; positive is favourable to the wallet.
  • ALO, IOC, GTC: order types: ALO is post-only (rejected if it would cross), IOC is immediate-or-cancel, GTC rests until cancelled.
  • Submits, cancels: new limit orders and cancels. The venue records a modify as one cancel plus one new order, so cancels per submit sits near 1.

5.3 Inventory scale and outcomes

Terms used here: Markout M30, M60, M120, rho
  • Markout M30, M60, M120: what a fill is worth against the mid 30, 60 or 120 minutes later, in bps of the fill's USD; positive is favourable to the wallet.
